title: Social Security claiming strategy
summary: Claiming at 62 vs. 67 vs. 70 is one of the largest financial decisions most retirees make. The "right" answer is almost never 62.
detailsHtml:
The math

Claiming at age 62 (the earliest) results in a permanent reduction of roughly 25–30% versus your Full Retirement Age (FRA, currently 67 for most workers). Claiming at 70 results in a permanent increase of roughly 24–32% versus FRA. The breakeven age for delaying from 62 to 70 is approximately 80–82 — meaning if you live past 82, delaying wins; if you don't, claiming early wins.

Why most analyses favor delay

Average life expectancy at age 62 (conditional on having reached 62) is 82 for men and 85 for women in the U.S. For couples, the probability of at least one spouse living past 82 is much higher than for an individual. Social Security is inflation-protected and provides longevity insurance the rest of your portfolio doesn't. For the higher earner in a couple, delaying often makes sense even if individual breakeven is uncertain, because the survivor benefit is also permanently increased.

Exceptions: Poor health with shortened life expectancy, immediate financial need with no alternative income, or planned Roth conversions in early retirement (where lower Social Security income lets you convert more at lower brackets) can all justify claiming earlier than 70.
SS interacts with IRMAA — see node 10.1. Claiming Social Security increases MAGI in the claim year and forward, which can push a household into a higher Medicare IRMAA tier (cliff structure, 2-year lookback). For households planning Roth conversions, the conversion size and the claiming-age decision are joint optimization problems — claiming late while converting aggressively in the bridge years is the standard high-leverage decumulation play; claiming early at 62 with simultaneous large conversions is the most common way to inadvertently land in the second or third IRMAA tier.
